templates.name: Addition/similarity: a further item of the same kind
Contrast: established view or appearance, then a finding that breaks it
Contrast: positive claim, then a limiting fact about the same subject
Cause/effect: condition, principle or evidence, then its consequence
Cause/effect: need or judgment, then the action it motivates
Concession: grant, then the main claim resumes (but / Still)
Concession: supported claim, then a fact that qualifies it
Purpose and aptness: goal then deliberate act, or a fitting echo
Specification/restatement: exact content or plain rewording
Sequence/time: next step, earlier or later event, end of a long effort
Culmination, alternative and place (ultimately, alternatively, there)
Example: general claim, then one named instance

items.passage: Planetary scientists classify Uranus and Neptune as “ice giants,” distinguishing them from the gas giants Jupiter and Saturn. ______ the water, ammonia, and methane that constitute their bulk are not frozen in the everyday sense but exist as a hot, dense fluid. Still, the classification is apt: these compounds were solid ices in the frigid outer solar system where both planets originally formed.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first sentence gives the classification “ice giants.” The blank sentence admits a point that seems to undercut the label: the planets’ ices are really a hot fluid. The next sentence turns back with “Still,” saying the label fits after all. “Admittedly” introduces a point the writer concedes before returning to the main claim.

A.why_wrong: The blank sentence does not spell out what “ice giants” means; it says the material is not ice in the everyday sense, which is why the following sentence has to defend the label with “Still.”

B.why_wrong: “Moreover” would add a further point in support of the label, but a hot, dense fluid is a reason to doubt the label, not to accept it.

D.why_wrong: Being classified as ice giants does not cause the planets’ water, ammonia, and methane to be a hot fluid; the name is not the source of their makeup.

items.notes: Grant then turn, the turn in the next sentence opened by Still (3.19 shape), keyed Admittedly (Of course and Granted are already common K1 keys in the bank). K1 has no band-7 official items (spec/rw/band7/transitions.md section 5), so this is written as a strong band 6 and band_target is 6, not the 7 the plan asked for. Trap: Specifically, since the blank sentence names what the planets are made of. No In fact or Indeed beside the concession key. Facts from general knowledge; not web-checked (Transitions, brief of 2026-10-16); no made-up finding attributed to a real person or organisation.

items.passage: In a 2002 review of nearly a hundred studies, psychologists Hillary Anger Elfenbein and Nalini Ambady found that people can recognize anger, fear, happiness, and other emotions displayed by members of unfamiliar cultures far more often than chance would predict. ______ people were noticeably less accurate with members of unfamiliar cultures than with members of their own culture.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first sentence reports that people recognize emotions across cultures far better than chance. The blank sentence limits that finding without overturning it: people are noticeably less accurate with unfamiliar cultures than with their own. “That said” introduces a fact that qualifies the claim just made.

A.why_wrong: Recognizing other cultures’ emotions above chance does not cause people to be less accurate with those cultures than with their own; the second result limits the first.

B.why_wrong: The blank sentence is not a rewording of the finding about other cultures; it adds a new comparison that shows a shortfall, unfamiliar cultures against one’s own.

C.why_wrong: “Moreover” would add a second point backing the claim that emotion recognition crosses cultures, but lower accuracy with unfamiliar cultures is a limit on that claim.

items.notes: Supported claim from a named study, then a result of the same study that qualifies it (3.8 shape). Band 6 by plan. No In fact or Indeed on offer (second-sense rule). Real study (Elfenbein and Ambady 2002, Psychological Bulletin meta-analysis, 97 studies, in-group advantage) known well enough to state; Facts from general knowledge; not web-checked (Transitions, brief of 2026-10-16); no made-up finding attributed to a real person or organisation.

fixes: plainer wording to bring the passage nearer CB register (5.61 to 5.48 chars per word): "analysis" to "review", "with accuracy well above chance" to "far more often than chance would predict", "cultural group" to "culture"
review.note: Transitions: no fact-checking by rule; rw_options finds no second acceptable connective; real named psychologists carry their real 2002 meta-analysis result (above-chance recognition with an in-group advantage); nothing invented

band7.why: K2 can reach band 7 (3.12, That said), but here the limit ("noticeably less accurate") cuts directly against "far more often than chance", a plainer turn than 3.12's record of no net energy gain under a long-held belief. Decoys Thus, In other words and Moreover each attach a plausible misreading (Moreover as a second result of the same study), with no adversative rival. Band 6 as planned, on a par with 3.8 and 3.14.

items.passage: Bees are usually pictured as the principal pollinators of flowering plants, carrying pollen from blossom to blossom as they feed. A study of the insects visiting flowers in northeast Greenland, however, found little support for that picture in the high Arctic; ______ the researchers reported, pollen there was transported by flies, predominantly members of the same family as the common housefly.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The clause before the blank says the Greenland study did not support the picture of bees as the main pollinators. The clause after it says what the researchers found instead was the usual case: flies carried the pollen. “More often” signals that this is the more common situation, compared with bees doing the work.

A.why_wrong: The study’s finding is not what made flies carry pollen; the clause after the blank reports what the study observed, not a result of the study.

C.why_wrong: “Nonetheless” would mean flies carried pollen in spite of the study’s doubts about bees, but the flies are the very reason the study doubts the picture.

D.why_wrong: The flies are not a second, separate finding added to the first; they are the content of the finding that the bee picture does not hold in the Arctic.

items.notes: Band-7 S1 frequency form (spec/rw/band7/transitions.md section 5): a popular picture, a however clause saying a study does not bear it out, then after a semicolon and the interrupter the researchers reported, the common case keyed more often. Moves: frequency key read off the comparison with no figure to read it from; surface contrast (flies, not bees, right after a however clause) pulls nonetheless; in addition pulls because B looks like a second finding; key outside the core 13; no sequence or summary decoy. Varied from earlier S1 items: subject is a pollinator survey, decoys as a result / nonetheless / in addition. Study (Tiusanen et al. 2016, muscid flies as key pollinators at Zackenberg) not named in the passage; Facts from general knowledge; not web-checked (Transitions, brief of 2026-10-16); no made-up finding attributed to a real person or organisation. Review: structurally a close copy of official d3b7d7a3 (popular account, then a however clause about a study, then a semicolon and the frequency key with a researchers-reported interrupter); check_rw finds no shared wording, so it stands as the section-5 recipe intends.

fixes: dropped the year from "A 2016 study" so the frame mirrors official d3b7d7a3 ("a 2016 study of 1940 census data") less closely; register unchanged
review.note: Transitions: no fact-checking by rule; rw_options finds no second acceptable connective; no named person carries an invented finding

band7.why: S1 frequency form from section 5, modelled on band-7 d3b7d7a3. Section 6 gates: key more often is outside the core 13; no sequence or summary decoy; surface-contrast proxy passes (key not adversative, nonetheless offered, "however" in the blank's own sentence); register 5.41 chars per word (at least 5.3); 61 words, blank after a semicolon and a researchers-reported interrupter. Decoy pull: flies, not bees, right after a however clause reads as a contrast to a hurried reader, so nonetheless attracts; in addition attracts as a second finding of the study. The key is read off an implied comparison (more often than bees) with no figure or wording in the passage that names it.

items.passage: Iceland’s constitution, adopted in 1944, was largely based on Denmark’s. After the 2008 financial crisis, the country’s parliament decided that it should be revised with direct input from ordinary citizens, not by politicians alone. ______ the twenty-five-member council chosen in 2011 to draft a new constitution posted its drafts online each week and invited public commentary.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The second sentence states a goal: a constitution revised with direct input from ordinary citizens. The blank sentence describes a deliberate step taken to reach that goal, posting drafts online so the public could comment. “To that end” introduces an action taken to achieve a stated aim.

B.why_wrong: “Nevertheless” would mean the council asked for public comment in spite of the goal of public input, but asking for comment is exactly what that goal called for.

C.why_wrong: The blank sentence does not reword the parliament’s decision; it reports a separate action by the drafting council that carried the decision out.

D.why_wrong: Posting drafts for comment is not a further, independent point beside the decision; it is the means by which the decision was put into practice.

items.passage: Musicians have long debated how to tune a scale. In just intonation, each interval is tuned to a simple whole-number ratio of frequencies, so chords in a single key sound perfectly consonant; ______ equal temperament divides the octave into twelve identical steps, leaving every interval except the octave slightly impure but permitting music to modulate freely between keys.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The sentence sets two tuning systems side by side. Just intonation gives pure chords in one key; equal temperament gives up that purity in exchange for freedom to change keys. “By contrast” signals that the second system differs from the first on the same point.

A.why_wrong: Equal temperament is not an instance of just intonation or of its pure chords; it is a different system with the opposite result.

B.why_wrong: Tuning intervals to whole-number ratios does not cause equal temperament to divide the octave into equal steps; the second system is an alternative to the first, not its result.

C.why_wrong: The two systems are built the same way in the sentence, but they do opposite things: one keeps intervals pure, the other makes them slightly impure.

items.notes: Two approaches, contrast keyed after a semicolon (3.18 shape). C1 has no band-7 official items (spec/rw/band7/transitions.md section 5), so this is a strong band 6 and band_target is 6, not the 7 the plan asked for. Facts from general knowledge; not web-checked (Transitions, brief of 2026-10-16); no made-up finding attributed to a real person or organisation.

items.passage: Seed banks conserve botanical diversity by desiccating seeds and storing them at subzero temperatures, conditions that orthodox seeds, including those of wheat and legumes, tolerate for decades. Recalcitrant seeds, ______ perish when they lose substantial moisture, so the seeds of avocado, cacao, and numerous tropical trees cannot be conserved this way.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first sentence says orthodox seeds survive being dried and frozen. The second says recalcitrant seeds die when they dry out. “By contrast” marks the second kind of seed as the opposite of the first on the same point.

B.why_wrong: Recalcitrant seeds are not an example of orthodox seeds or of seeds that survive drying; they are the kind that does not survive it.

C.why_wrong: Recalcitrant seeds do not behave like orthodox seeds; one kind survives drying and freezing and the other dies.

D.why_wrong: The fact that orthodox seeds survive storage does not cause recalcitrant seeds to die when dried; the two kinds simply respond in opposite ways.

items.notes: Two subjects, one attribute, opposite values, the connective as an interrupter after the second subject (2.6 shape). Facts from general knowledge; not web-checked (Transitions, brief of 2026-10-16); no made-up finding attributed to a real person or organisation.

review.note: Transitions: no fact-checking by rule; rw_options finds no second acceptable connective; no named person carries an invented finding

items.passage: Finnish composer Einojuhani Rautavaara subtitled his 1972 work Cantus Arcticus “Concerto for Birds and Orchestra.” The piece pairs a live orchestra with recordings of birdsong made near the Arctic Circle, letting the musicians accompany the birds. ______ American composer Alan Hovhaness’s And God Created Great Whales (1970) sets an orchestra against recorded humpback whale songs.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first sentence describes a work that combines an orchestra with recorded birdsong. The second describes a different work that does the same thing with recorded whale songs. “Likewise” signals that the second case parallels the first.

A.why_wrong: Nothing about Rautavaara’s piece would lead one to expect Hovhaness not to use recorded animal sounds, so there is nothing for the second sentence to hold true in spite of.

B.why_wrong: The second sentence does not give more precise details about Cantus Arcticus; it turns to a separate work by another composer.

D.why_wrong: Rautavaara’s 1972 piece could not have led to Hovhaness’s 1970 piece, and the passage gives no causal link between the two works.

items.notes: Similarity key: a second work doing the same thing as the first (2.7 shape, two members of one set). No addition decoy beside a similarity key. Facts from general knowledge; not web-checked (Transitions, brief of 2026-10-16); no made-up finding attributed to a real person or organisation.

review.note: Transitions: no fact-checking by rule; rw_options finds no second acceptable connective; Rautavaara and Hovhaness works described as they are; no invented finding

items.passage: Baleen whales lack the teeth that biologists examine to estimate a mammal’s age, so researchers rely on alternative evidence. They count the layers in a whale’s earwax plug, which accumulates a light and a dark layer approximately every year. ______ they measure chemical alterations in proteins of the eye’s lens, alterations that proceed at a steady rate.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The passage says researchers use other evidence to age whales. The second sentence gives one method, counting earwax layers, and the blank sentence gives a second, separate method, measuring changes in the eye’s lens. “Additionally” introduces a further item of the same kind.

A.why_wrong: Measuring changes in the eye’s lens is not a rewording of counting earwax layers; it is a different technique.

C.why_wrong: “Nevertheless” would mean researchers measure the lens in spite of counting earwax layers, but the two methods do not work against each other.

D.why_wrong: Counting earwax layers does not lead to or require measuring the eye’s lens; the second method is independent of the first.

items.passage: Stockfish, the dried cod for which Norway’s Lofoten Islands are renowned, is preserved exclusively by the climate. ______ after the cod are harvested in late winter, they are gutted, fastened in pairs, and suspended on wooden racks outdoors. There they remain for approximately three months while the frigid, dry wind dehydrates them.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first sentence makes a general claim: stockfish is preserved by the climate alone. The blank sentence and the one after it spell out exactly how: the fish hang outdoors until the wind dries them. “Specifically” introduces the precise details of the general claim.

A.why_wrong: Hanging fish outdoors in the cold, dry wind does not contrast with preservation by the weather; it is the preservation by climate that the first sentence describes.

B.why_wrong: The drying on outdoor racks is not a consequence of stockfish being preserved by the climate; it is the process the first sentence refers to.

C.why_wrong: The blank sentence does not add a separate fact about stockfish; it describes the same preservation the first sentence mentions.

items.notes: General claim, then its exact content (2.12 shape). No example or restatement decoy beside a specification key. Facts from general knowledge; not web-checked (Transitions, brief of 2026-10-16); no made-up finding attributed to a real person or organisation.

items.passage: The ghost pipe, a woodland plant of Asia and the Americas, lacks chlorophyll, the pigment that enables plants to harness energy from sunlight. It obtains carbohydrates instead from subterranean fungi, which extract them from the roots of neighboring trees. ______ the ghost pipe can flourish on forest floors too shaded for most photosynthesizing plants.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The passage explains that the ghost pipe does not need sunlight for energy, because it gets its sugars from fungi. The blank sentence gives the result: it can grow where there is too little light for most plants. “Hence” introduces a consequence of what came before.

B.why_wrong: Growing in deep shade is not surprising given what came before; a plant that gets its sugars from fungi rather than sunlight is exactly the kind that can live in the shade.

C.why_wrong: Flourishing on dark forest floors is not an instance of the plant drawing sugars from fungi; it is what that habit makes possible.

D.why_wrong: The blank sentence does not describe a second plant or behavior like the one before; it tells what follows from the ghost pipe’s way of feeding.

items.notes: Condition, then its consequence across two sentences (2.9 shape). The instead in sentence 2 sits before the blank but marks the plant’s alternative food source, not the relation the blank tests. Facts from general knowledge; not web-checked (Transitions, brief of 2026-10-16); no made-up finding attributed to a real person or organisation.

items.passage: British writer Roy Moxham spent years searching for remnants of the Great Hedge of India, a barrier of thorny vegetation that colonial authorities cultivated in the 1800s to obstruct the smuggling of untaxed salt. Several expeditions guided by nineteenth-century maps proved unsuccessful. ______ in 1998, he located a short surviving stretch in Uttar Pradesh.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The passage describes years of searching and several expeditions that failed. The blank sentence reports that the search at last succeeded in 1998. “Finally” marks the end of a long effort.

A.why_wrong: The unsuccessful expeditions did not produce the 1998 discovery; the discovery came after them, ending the search.

B.why_wrong: Finding a surviving stretch is not a rewording of searching without success; it is the opposite outcome, reached later.

D.why_wrong: The 1998 discovery is not similar to the failed expeditions; it is the success that ended them.

items.notes: Years of failure, then the end of the effort keyed Finally (2.13 shape). No adversative on offer, since However or Nevertheless would also fit a failure followed by success. items.passage: Salmon and sea turtles are known to return to their birthplaces to reproduce, but such natal homing had never been documented in sharks. During a nineteen-year investigation at the Bahamian island of Bimini, ______ researchers determined that female lemon sharks returned to give birth in the very lagoon where they themselves had been born.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first sentence says homing to a birthplace had never been documented in sharks. The second reports a study that found exactly that in lemon sharks. “However” signals that the new finding goes against what had been known before.

A.why_wrong: The lemon shark finding is not an example of homing never being confirmed in sharks; it is the first confirmation.

C.why_wrong: The study’s result does not reword the first sentence; it reports something new that the first sentence said had not yet been shown.

D.why_wrong: The lack of earlier evidence in sharks is not what caused female lemon sharks to return to their birth lagoon.

items.notes: Known pattern and an unconfirmed case, then the finding, with the connective after an introductory phrase (2.1 shape). No similarity or addition decoy, since the finding parallels the salmon and turtles. Researchers unnamed. B.why_wrong: The translation is not an example of the Dutch book’s accuracy or of Sugita’s judgment; it is the step he took because of that judgment.

C.why_wrong: The blank sentence does not reword Sugita’s conclusion; it reports a new action that followed from it.

items.passage: In 1865, Italian physicist Giovanni Caselli opened the first commercial service for sending images over telegraph wires, linking Paris and Lyon with a machine he called the pantelegraph. ______ in 1843, Scottish inventor Alexander Bain had patented a device that used swinging pendulums to copy images line by line from one place to another.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first sentence describes an event of 1865. The blank sentence describes one that happened before it, in 1843, and uses “had patented” to show that it came first. “Earlier” signals that the second event took place before the first.

A.why_wrong: Caselli’s 1865 service could not have caused something that happened in 1843.

B.why_wrong: Bain’s patent is not a rewording of Caselli’s service; it is a different event by a different inventor.

C.why_wrong: “Next” would place Bain’s patent after Caselli’s service, but 1843 came before 1865.

items.notes: Reverse chronology with dates and a past perfect (1.12 shape). No similarity decoy, since Bain’s device resembles Caselli’s machine. Facts from general knowledge; not web-checked (Transitions, brief of 2026-10-16); no made-up finding attributed to a real person or organisation.

items.passage: The Arctic woolly bear caterpillar inhabits the northernmost regions of Greenland and Canada, where summers are brief and temperatures remain low. It can feed for only a few weeks each year before freezing solid for the long winter. ______ the caterpillar develops slowly, taking about seven years to become a moth.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The passage says the caterpillar can feed for only a few weeks a year. The blank sentence gives the result: it grows slowly and needs about seven years to become a moth. “As a result” introduces a consequence of what came before.

A.why_wrong: Slow growth does not contrast with a short feeding season; it is what a short feeding season leads to.

C.why_wrong: The caterpillar’s slow growth did not happen before its feeding and freezing; it happens over the same years.

D.why_wrong: Taking seven years to become a moth is not an example of feeding for a few weeks; it is the outcome of it.

items.notes: Condition, then its consequence (1.5 shape). Facts from general knowledge; not web-checked (Transitions, brief of 2026-10-16); no made-up finding attributed to a real person or organisation.

fixes: plainer wording ("annually" to "each year", "requiring about seven years to transform into" to "taking about seven years to become"); 5.29 to 5.07 chars per word

items.passage: Italian painter Sofonisba Anguissola achieved international fame during her lifetime. In 1559, she was invited to the Spanish court of King Philip II, where she painted portraits of the royal family for more than a decade. ______ after her death, many of her paintings were attributed to male artists, and her reputation gradually faded.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first two sentences describe Anguissola’s fame and success while she was alive. The blank sentence says that after her death her work was credited to others and her reputation faded. “However” signals this contrast.

A.why_wrong: Her fame in her lifetime did not cause her paintings to be credited to other artists later.

B.why_wrong: Losing credit for her portraits is not one more sign of her fame; it works against it.

D.why_wrong: The passage is not listing points in order, so there is no first point for a second one to follow.

items.notes: Fame then neglect (1.10 shape). Facts from general knowledge; not web-checked (Transitions, brief of 2026-10-16); no made-up finding attributed to a real person or organisation.

review.note: Transitions: no fact-checking by rule; rw_options finds no second acceptable connective; Anguissola is real; no invented finding

items.passage: Argentine writer Julio Cortázar’s 1963 novel Hopscotch offers readers two different experiences. Readers who prefer a conventional narrative can read chapters 1 through 56 in order and stop. Those who follow the author’s “table of instructions,” ______ begin with chapter 73 and jump around the book in a sequence Cortázar specifies.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The passage describes two ways to read the novel. One group reads chapters 1 through 56 in order; the other begins at chapter 73 and jumps around. “By contrast” signals that the second way of reading differs from the first.

B.why_wrong: Starting at chapter 73 is not an example of reading chapters 1 through 56 in order; it is the other way to read the book.

C.why_wrong: Some readers reading the chapters in order does not cause other readers to begin at chapter 73.

D.why_wrong: The second way of reading is not like the first; one goes straight through and the other jumps around.

items.notes: Two groups, opposite ways, connective as an interrupter after the second subject (1.34 shape). Facts from general knowledge; not web-checked (Transitions, brief of 2026-10-16); no made-up finding attributed to a real person or organisation.

items.passage: About 5,000 years ago, Neolithic farmers constructed the village of Skara Brae on Orkney, an archipelago off the northern coast of Scotland. Few trees grew on the windswept islands, and timber was extremely scarce. ______ the villagers built their beds, shelves, and dressers from flat slabs of local stone, many of which survive today.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The second sentence says that timber was scarce on the islands. The blank sentence describes what the villagers did because of that: they made their furniture from stone. “For this reason” introduces an action taken because of what came before.

A.why_wrong: Making furniture from stone is not similar to timber being scarce; it is the villagers’ response to the shortage.

C.why_wrong: Using stone does not contrast with a lack of timber; it follows from it.

D.why_wrong: Building furniture from stone is not a rewording of timber being scarce; it is what the villagers did about the shortage.

items.passage: When Mexican artist Juan O’Gorman designed the enormous mosaic that covers the exterior walls of the Central Library at the National Autonomous University of Mexico, he wanted its colors to remain vivid for centuries. ______ he constructed the mosaic from naturally colored stones collected from different regions of Mexico rather than from paint.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first sentence states O’Gorman’s goal: colors that would stay vivid for centuries. The blank sentence describes what he did to reach that goal: he used naturally colored stones. “To that end” introduces an action taken to achieve a stated aim.

A.why_wrong: Using colored stones does not contrast with wanting lasting colors; it is how O’Gorman achieved them.

B.why_wrong: The blank sentence does not reword O’Gorman’s goal; it describes the material he chose to meet it.

D.why_wrong: The blank sentence does not sum up the passage; it adds a new fact about how the mosaic was made.

items.notes: Goal, then the deliberate act that serves it (1.21 shape). No cause/effect decoy beside a purpose key. Facts from general knowledge; not web-checked (Transitions, brief of 2026-10-16); no made-up finding attributed to a real person or organisation.
